about: The built environments chapter experiences can be staged in (interpreter/internal/chapters). 'scripted' environments have manifests and take a SceneScript (props, clips, lights, sounds per sentence); 'place' environments are rooms the reader inhabits, adapted by mood and haze only. Triangles and meshes are the measured counts from the Blender builds (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md). A chapter whose setting none of these can honestly stand for is reported as having no place built yet, never staged somewhere unrelated.

environments.place: A long, low hall lined with locked doors, lamps hanging from the roof; a three-legged glass table, a low curtain with a little door behind it.
A long table laid for tea under a great tree in front of a house, chairs and cups crowded at one corner, afternoon light.
A formal rose garden and croquet lawn: hedges, a rose tree, gravel paths, open sky.
Inside a one-room Kansas farmhouse on the gray prairie: a cooking stove, a cupboard, a table, beds, a trapdoor to the cyclone cellar; the flat prairie outside.
The nymph Calypso's cave on the island of Ogygia: a fire on the hearth, a loom, vines and a garden with springs outside the mouth, the sea beyond.
A farmhouse bedroom in Brobdingnag seen at Gulliver's size: the reader stands on a giant table among enormous furniture, a candle and a window far above.

The grassy top of a river bank in the land of Oz on a late, sunny afternoon: a great meadow of scarlet poppies spreads away to the left and towards the horizon; a broad, slow river runs below a short earth bank on the right with reeds and stones, alders and willows on the far side; fruit trees along the near bank; a faint green glow on the horizon where the Emerald City lies.

The Throne Room in the Palace of Oz: a big, round room with a high arched roof; walls, roof and floor covered with large emeralds set closely together between green marble pilasters; a great light as bright as the sun in the centre of the roof; in the middle, on a round stepped dais, the big empty throne of green marble set with gems; a little door from the south and a green silk screen against the wall.

The stern deck of a black Bronze-Age ship lying still in a dead calm off the Sirens' island on a hazy summer morning: rowing benches with oars shipped, the mast with its cross piece and lashings, the furled sail, twin steering oars, a cut wheel of wax and a bronze sword on the deck; off the port bow a small island with a limestone cliff, a field of flowers falling to a cove and a pale heap of bones.

The great hall of Odysseus's house at Ithaca early on a winter feast-day morning: a round hearth with a newly lit fire among four cypress bearing-posts, a smoke-lantern open to the sky above it, smoke-blackened walls with pale shapes and empty pegs where the armour hung, tables and purple-covered seats along the walls, a bronze mixing-bowl by the door into the house, a stair to the upper room, low sunlight through the porch and the high ash-wood threshold.

Lilliput seen at Gulliver's size on a clear early-summer morning: short soft turf before the north gate of the ancient temple, chains running from its little window, tents and the empty engine on the common; across the highway a five-foot turret, then hedged fields forty feet square like beds of flowers, small woods of seven-foot trees, the walled town on the left like a painted theatre scene, and to the right a low bank, a pale beach and the sea with two men of war at anchor.

A stone gallery on the rim of Laputa, the flying island, on a clear mid-morning: a half-octagonal belvedere behind a waist-high limestone balustrade with a brass telescope; below, lower galleries and stairs step down to the adamant verge where an iron davit hangs its chain and seat over the void; two miles beneath, through haze and scattered cumulus, the fields, river, villages and coast of Balnibarbi; behind, galleries rise in tiers to the upper garden.

The Battery at the tip of Manhattan on a breezy September afternoon (Moby-Dick, chapter 1, Loomings): the granite mole with its iron railing, a gravel promenade with empty benches and gas lamps, elms and lawns, the brick houses of State Street behind; Castle Garden on its footbridge flying its flag; ships at anchor and the East River piers; Governors Island, Staten Island and the Jersey and Brooklyn shores across the bay.

The Spouter-Inn at New Bedford on a December night (Moby-Dick, chapters 2-5 and 10-11): a low, wide, wainscoted entry with the besmoked oil painting, a wall of South Sea clubs and spears, rusty harpoons and lances, a carved settle and a tall clock; through a low arch in the old chimney the public room with its iron box stove, the bar built into a right whale's jaw, a long table under glass cases, tallow candles and lanterns.

The Pequod's quarter-deck at the Nantucket wharf on a cold December noon (Moby-Dick, chapters 16-22): an old weather-stained whaler, her open bulwarks garnished with sperm-whale teeth for belaying pins, the tiller carved from a whale's lower jaw, the wigwam of right-whale bone abaft the mainmast with Captain Peleg's chair, the try-works, three masts with furled sails and full rigging; the wharf with spiles, oil casks and sheds, the town and the far shore, old snow in the waterways.

Ogilvy's observatory at Ottershaw at midnight in August (The War of the Worlds, chapter 1): a small timber observatory with its dome slit open to the stars and Mars low in the slit, a brass refractor on an equatorial mount with its clockwork drive, a shuttered lantern glowing in a corner, a little table with a siphon, a desk with a star chart and a clock.

The sand pits on Horsell Common just after an August sunrise (The War of the Worlds, chapters 2-5): a heathery knoll at the lip of the pit, the huge cylinder half buried in flung sand with its crust flaking from the end, splinters of a shivered fir round the rim, Scots pines, heather, gorse and bracken, and a thread of smoke rising from burning heather in the dawn sky.

The narrator's dining room in a villa at Maybury on a summer evening at dusk (The War of the Worlds, chapters 7-8): a table laid with a white cloth, silver, glass and a cold dinner, a decanter of claret, an oil lamp under a pink shade; a low fire in a tiled grate under a slate mantel with a clock and candlesticks; a sash window onto the darkening garden between velvet curtains; sideboard, oil paintings, a Turkey carpet.

The cove below the Admiral Benbow inn on a frosty January dawn (Treasure Island, chapters 1-5): grey slate cliffs, a rounded shingle beach white with hoar-frost, a big rock at the turn of the beach, the sea washing in, and the combe climbing to the inn and its swinging signboard.

The library at Squire Trelawney's Hall on a moonlit winter night (Treasure Island, chapter 6, The Captain's Papers): mahogany bookcases filled with books and topped by marble busts, a fire burning in the chimneypiece, wing chairs, the library table with the oilskin packet, the account book and the map of the island with its red crosses, a globe, a longcase clock, sash windows onto the moonlit avenue.

The Spy-glass tavern on the Bristol docks on a bright morning (Treasure Island, chapters 7-8): a large, low, whitewashed room under heavy oak beams with a sanded floor, trestle tables with pewter, pipes and cards, the bar with casks and bottles, a small fire and red curtains; doors open onto the cobbled quay with the brass telescope sign, a moored ship with rigging and figurehead, and a forest of masts across the harbour.

Mr Bennet's library at Longbourn by day (Pride and Prejudice, e.g. chapters 2, 15, 20, 57 and 59): walls of book-lined shelving, a writing table at the window with an open folio, two chairs under a county map, a globe, a coal fire in the grate, and a view of the lane outside.

The footpath across the fields from Longbourn to Netherfield after rain (Pride and Prejudice, chapter 7, Elizabeth's walk): ridge-and-furrow pasture, laid hedgerows with oak and ash, a stile and a gate, puddles on the muddy path, rooks over the trees, and Netherfield House across the park under a clearing sky.

The drawing-room at Netherfield in the evening by candle and firelight (Pride and Prejudice, chapters 8-11): a loo table with a card game in progress, a marble chimney-piece with a coal fire, a table of books, chairs and a sofa, a mirror, and curtains drawn across the tall windows.
